title: Louis Jordan the man, and his hit repertoire
summary: Jordan was a very nice man who used to come to Warren with his father's Rabbit Foot show; Phillips lists his hits and says Southern audiences loved the blues.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it

blocks.x: Any interesting comments that Louis Jordan made that you might want to pass on?

Oh, he was a nice guy. He was a really nice guy. He was just about as nice a fellow as you'd want to meet. Because, see, I didn't know him too much in Arkansas, because he lived in one part of Arkansas and I lived in
another; he lived in northern Arkansas and I lived in southern Arkansas. But anyway, he used to come to my home all the time on his Daddy's show...
I guess it was a really influential little group at that time.

Oh yeah. We were playing everything. He was playing then "Caledonia," "Choo-Choo Cha-Boogie," "Slender, Tender and Tall," "Salt Pork, West Virginia," "Ain't Nobody Here But Us Chickens," "I'm Gonna Move to The Outskirts of Town" -- that's the tune that made him. If you went to a dance, you didn't have to play too much, because you'd play "I'm Gonna Move..." -- man, he'd play that for about an hour. And them people still... Especially when you'd go down South, they'd be screamin' and hollerin' about that, because that's the Blues! People down South understand the Blues. They know the Blues. Like me, I know the Blues. I know all kind of Blues. There's dirty low-down Blues and there's kind of a moderate Blues.
